narrative: Today's batch highlights several fire-ecology findings: camera-trap occupancy modelling in a Namibian savanna shows mammal communities decline steadily in burned areas with no refuge effect in adjacent zones, while tree-ring evidence traces a 19th-century pulse of Appalachian fire activity to industrialisation. In movement and behaviour, GPS tracking shows a barrier-aware model outperforms simple geometric estimators for urban hedgehog home ranges, and free-ranging lizards were shown to actively regulate UV exposure as a physiological axis distinct from thermoregulation. Two invasional-meltdown studies stand out: reduced litter allelochemicals let established alien plants facilitate further invasions, and an introduced pagoda tree is shown to facilitate spread of the giant resin bee. On the conservation and landscape side, GPS-collared caribou selected regenerating clearcuts despite elevated predator activity there, functioning as ecological traps, while a new landscape-optimisation framework identifies trade-off zones balancing food production against ecological protection in China. In methods, a new evolutionary algorithm (ESO) shrinks bioacoustic classifiers for real-time passive monitoring, and drone-derived elevation data improved species distribution models for a mountain primate over coarser satellite products. A long-running Arctic tundra study also found earthworms extend late-season photosynthesis, boosting winter carbon uptake except after severe drought.
